notes: Photography-style knowledge base. Each style: 'recipe' = recommended starting settings + why (frontend can auto-apply via snapToCamera); 'priorities' = multipliers for the heuristic coach's score penalties (highlights, shadows, exposure, color_cast, noise, sharpness); 'rules' = deterministic nudges applied to recommendations (shutter_floor, aperture_target, iso_max, allow_slow_shutter); 'exercises' = style-specific drills (shown first, max 2, rest filled generically). Add a style by appending an object — no code changes.

styles.label: Landscape
styles.description: Captures natural or urban scenes, emphasizing scale and mood. This genre often features wide vistas or intimate details, showcasing the beauty of the environment.

recipe.summary: Mid-aperture sweet spot, base ISO, shutter can go slow on a tripod.
recipe.why: f/8–f/11 is most lenses' sharpness sweet spot and holds front-to-back detail; base ISO maximizes dynamic range so the sky and shadows both survive; on a tripod the shutter can stretch as long as the light wants.

watch_fors: Sky far brighter than the land — the sky clips before the ground is exposed.
Everything slightly soft — diffraction past f/16 or focus not set near the hyperfocal distance.
Horizon dead-center flattening the frame — try thirds and a foreground anchor.

exercises.title: Thirds horizon
exercises.goal: Shoot the same scene with the horizon on the top third, bottom third, and center.
exercises.how: Compare which framing carries the scene: dramatic sky → horizon low; interesting foreground → horizon high. Note your instinct — then break it on purpose next time.

exercises.title: Front anchor
exercises.goal: Add depth with a deliberate foreground element.
exercises.how: Find a rock, path or flower 1–2 m from the camera, focus near the hyperfocal distance, and let it lead the eye to the background. Shoot with and without — depth is the difference.

styles.label: Macro
styles.description: Focuses on extreme close-ups of small subjects, such as insects or flowers. It reveals intricate textures and details that are often overlooked, making the ordinary appear extraordinary.

recipe.summary: Stop down for working depth of field, fast shutter to beat magnified shake, moderate ISO.
recipe.why: At macro distances depth of field is razor-thin even at f/8, so stopping down buys the only sharpness there is; 1/200s beats the magnified camera shake that close work exaggerates; ISO 400 covers the light you lose to the small aperture.

watch_fors: Depth of field a millimeter thin — the eyes sharp but the antennae gone.
Camera shake multiplied by magnification — every wobble shows.
Harsh on-board flash flattening the texture you came for.

exercises.title: Coin hunt
exercises.goal: Sharply capture a coin or stamp at closest focus.
exercises.how: Tripod, live-view magnification, and manual focus. Move the camera (not the focus ring) in tiny steps until the detail snaps — this teaches where your sharp plane lives.

exercises.title: Aperture ladder at 1:1
exercises.goal: See how f/4 vs f/8 vs f/16 changes a macro frame.
exercises.how: Photograph the same flower center at three apertures. Compare the petal edges at 100% — depth grows, but diffraction softens everything past f/16. Find your lens's macro sweet spot.

styles.label: Wildlife
styles.description: Documents animals in their natural habitats. This type requires patience and timing to capture the behavior and beauty of wildlife, often in remote locations.

recipe.summary: Long lens wide open, fast shutter for sudden movement, ISO floats upward.
recipe.why: Animals never pose twice: 1/1000s freezes the flick of a tail, the widest aperture you have gathers light in dawn forests, and ISO floats upward without guilt — a noisy wildlife frame beats a missed one every time.

watch_fors: Focus on the grass in front of the animal, not the eye.
Shutter too slow for a sudden sprint or wingbeat.
ISO pushed so high that grain eats fur and feather detail.

exercises.title: Backyard safari
exercises.goal: Get a sharp, eye-level frame of a bird or squirrel with the eye in focus.
exercises.how: Pre-focus on a perch it uses, then wait for the return. Pre-focus + patience beats chasing — and teaches you animal routines.

exercises.title: Shutter ladder, feathers edition
exercises.goal: Find the speed that freezes your subject's movement.
exercises.how: Shoot a bird at 1/250, 1/500, 1/1000, 1/2000. Wing tips blur first, eyes last. Note your threshold for perched vs flying subjects.

styles.label: Portrait
styles.description: Aims to reveal a person's character or identity through posed or candid images. It focuses on the subject, capturing emotions and personality.

recipe.summary: Wide aperture for background blur, shutter safe for handheld, lowest ISO the light allows.
recipe.why: f/1.8–f/2.8 melts the background so the person pops; 1/200s freezes subtle movement and camera shake; base ISO keeps skin tones clean — raise ISO only when the shutter would drop below 1/125.

watch_fors: Focus landed on the nose or cheek instead of the near eye.
Background not separating — aperture not wide enough, or subject too close to the background.
Indoor skin drifting orange — the white balance is fighting the room's bulbs.

exercises.title: Eye of the needle
exercises.goal: 10 portraits where the near eye is tack-sharp at f/2 or wider.
exercises.how: Use single-point AF placed on the near eye, shoot, then magnify playback to verify before moving on. Misses teach you your lens's focus behavior faster than anything else.

exercises.title: Distance beats aperture
exercises.goal: Prove that subject-to-background distance changes blur more than stopping down.
exercises.how: Photograph the same person twice at f/2.8: once with the background 2 m behind, once 10 m. Compare — then use it: pull your subject away from walls.

styles.label: Sports
styles.description: Requires fast autofocus and precise timing to capture action during games or events. This genre often involves dynamic scenes and movement, showcasing athleticism.

recipe.summary: Fast shutter first, continuous AF, open aperture, let ISO float.
recipe.why: 1/1000s freezes most human and pet motion; AF-C / AI Servo keeps focus tracking; a wide aperture pays for the fast shutter and ISO floats upward — a frozen, slightly noisy frame beats a clean blur every time.

watch_fors: Motion blur on hands, feet or the ball — shutter too slow for the speed of the action.
Focus snapped onto the crowd or fence behind the athlete.
Grain eating detail after chasing a fast shutter with ISO — acceptable trade, know your ceiling.

exercises.title: Shutter ladder
exercises.goal: Find the exact shutter that freezes your subject.
exercises.how: Shoot the same sprint/jump at 1/250, 1/500, 1/1000, 1/2000. Check hands and feet at 100% zoom — that's where blur shows first. Remember the number for that sport.

exercises.title: Panning practice
exercises.goal: Sharp subject, streaked background — the deliberate-blur look.
exercises.how: Set 1/30s, AF-C on the subject, and move the camera with them through the shot. Expect 1 keeper in 20 at first — it's a wrist skill.

styles.label: Astrophotography
styles.description: Uses long exposures to photograph celestial objects like stars and galaxies. This type often requires specialized equipment and techniques to capture the night sky's beauty.

recipe.summary: Tripod required: wide aperture, multi-second shutter, high-but-controlled ISO.
recipe.why: On a tripod the shutter collects starlight for seconds; the widest aperture gathers the most of it; ISO 1600–3200 balances noise against exposure. Start with the recipe, then adjust by test frames — digital film is free.

watch_fors: Stars smeared into short trails — shutter too long for the focal length (use the 500 rule: 500 ÷ focal length = max seconds).
Noise blooming in the shadows from high ISO.
Light pollution tinting the sky orange or green — a WB tweak or post fix.

exercises.title: 500-rule workout
exercises.goal: Find your lens's max star-sharp shutter.
exercises.how: With a tripod, shoot the same star field at 5s, 10s, 15s, 20s with a 24mm lens. Zoom to 100%: the shutter where stars stop being dots marks your limit (≈20s here).

exercises.title: Tripod discipline
exercises.goal: Learn the ritual that keeps long exposures crisp.
exercises.how: Tripod + 2s timer (or remote), no touching during exposure, mirror-up/EFCS if your camera has it. Repeat until sharp 5s handheld-impossible frames become routine.

styles.label: Street
styles.description: Candidly captures everyday life and people in public spaces. This genre focuses on spontaneous moments, often highlighting the human experience in urban settings.

recipe.summary: Everything ready before the moment: moderate aperture, safe shutter, floating ISO.
recipe.why: Street moments arrive in half a second: f/5.6 keeps a moving subject within the focus zone, 1/250s handles walking pace, and a floating ISO means you never miss while dialing — set it once, then only compose.

watch_fors: The decisive moment ruined by a half-pressed menu dive — settings should be set before you raise the camera.
Harsh midday light carving hollow eyes — watch where faces turn.
Cluttered edges stealing the story from the subject.

exercises.title: One corner, one hour
exercises.goal: Stay in one spot and photograph ten different moments.
exercises.how: Pick a busy corner and wait. Light changes, people layer, stories overlap — this drills patience and pre-set settings instead of chasing.

exercises.title: Zone focus drill
exercises.goal: Learn the working depth of f/5.6 at 2–4 meters.
exercises.how: Pre-focus to 3 m, then shoot subjects entering the zone without refocusing. Old street photographers did this by feel — the simulator shows you exactly how deep that zone is.

styles.label: Fine Art
styles.description: Emphasizes creative expression and the photographer's vision rather than literal representation. It allows for artistic interpretation and can encompass various subjects.

recipe.summary: Break the rules on purpose: small aperture and long exposure are your brushes.
recipe.why: Fine art often wants what documentary avoids: f/11 for dreamy softness at the edges, multi-second exposures that turn water and people into abstractions, and deliberate underexposure for mood. Here the 'wrong' settings are the style.

watch_fors: Blur that reads as accident instead of intention — commit to the effect.
mood so dark the shadows turn to mud — underexpose with purpose, not by mistake.
Over-processing chasing drama the frame doesn't have.

exercises.title: Make water smoke
exercises.goal: One long exposure that turns a waterfall or fountain into mist.
exercises.how: Tripod, f/11, ISO 100, and the slowest shutter the light allows (ND filter if you have one). The 2" preset here shows the effect instantly.

exercises.title: One subject, three moods
exercises.goal: Photograph the same scene bright/airy, dark/moody, and washed/soft.
exercises.how: Change only exposure comp and picture style between frames. Comparing them side by side teaches that 'correct' is a choice, not a setting.

styles.label: Event
styles.description: Documents gatherings such as weddings, concerts, and parties. This genre blends candid and posed shots to capture the essence of the event and its participants.

recipe.summary: Flexible mid-fast settings: f/2.8–f/4, 1/160s+, ISO floats, WB matched per room.
recipe.why: Venues mix daylight, tungsten and DJ lighting within minutes; f/2.8–f/4 keeps small groups sharp while gathering light; 1/160s survives the processional; a floating ISO matters less than missing the once-only moment.

watch_fors: The white dress or cake blowing out — bright subjects clip before anything else in the frame.
Mixed light making skin orange in one corner and green in another.
Group shots taken at slow shutter — 1/125s minimum, and check every face for blinks.

exercises.title: Mixed-light safari
exercises.goal: One room, three light sources, three WB decisions.
exercises.how: In a room with window light plus bulbs, shoot the same subject under each source with the matching WB preset. Builds the reflex to re-check WB every time the light changes.

exercises.title: Bright-subject guardian
exercises.goal: Keep the white dress, cake or bride's highlights detailed in every frame.
exercises.how: Enable highlight alert and expose so the brightest subject sits just under clipping, letting the rest go slightly dark — recover shadows in post far more easily than fabric texture.

styles.label: Architecture
styles.description: Highlights the design and details of buildings and structures. This type focuses on lines, shadows, and the overall aesthetic of architectural forms.

recipe.summary: Small aperture for edge-to-edge sharpness, low ISO, tripod-friendly slow shutter.
recipe.why: Buildings hold still, so you can buy everything: f/8–f/11 keeps every line crisp corner to corner, base ISO squeezes out maximum detail, and a tripod plus slow shutter turns mixed light into even, clean exposures. Watch the verticals — they're the genre's signature.

watch_fors: Keystoned verticals — walls leaning inward because you tilted the camera back.
Mixed window light vs daylight color patches across one facade.
Diffraction softening after f/16 — more stopping down isn't always sharper.

exercises.title: Straight lines drill
exercises.goal: Keep every vertical truly vertical in a full facade shot.
exercises.how: Shoot from directly in front at mid-building height, or embrace the tilt and shoot up on purpose. The point is choosing — accidental keystoning is what kills architectural frames.

exercises.title: Light chasing
exercises.goal: Photograph the same building at three times of day.
exercises.how: Morning, midday, golden hour. Compare how shadows define the form — architecture is a light-dependent subject wearing a static disguise.

styles.label: Underwater
styles.description: Shot in or under water — diving, snorkeling, pools. Water steals red light and contrast with every meter, so this genre is about getting close, adding light back, and keeping the subject sharp through a housing port.

recipe.summary: Close focus, f/5.6 for strobe depth, 1/160 to freeze surge, ISO 400 to spare the strobes.
recipe.why: Water eats red and contrast fast, so the fix is distance not exposure: get within a meter of the subject. f/5.6 holds depth on a moving reef subject, 1/160 freezes surge and fish jitter, and ISO 400 lets the strobes work at a distance they can actually reach.

watch_fors: Everything hazy blue-gray — too much water between lens and subject; move closer, then closer again.
Backscatter snow in the strobe light — angle strobes outward from the housing, not straight ahead.
Blue-cyan cast deepening with depth — white balance manually at depth or shoot RAW and fix it later.

exercises.title: Minimum water
exercises.goal: Feel why distance, not settings, makes underwater shots pop.
exercises.how: Simulate a reef scene and note the haze; the teaching point is that no f-stop fixes water contrast. In the field, fill the frame with the subject before you touch a dial.

exercises.title: Strobe drag
exercises.goal: Balance ambient exposure against strobe reach.
exercises.how: Drop the shutter (more ambient blue) then raise it (darker, strobe-defined) and watch the color story change. Underwater exposure is two exposures in one frame.

styles.label: Food
styles.description: Editorial and menu photography of dishes. Soft directional light, tight apertures around f/4–f/8 for appetite appeal, and color accuracy that makes the dish look edible.

recipe.summary: Tripod base ISO, f/4–f/8, slow shutter welcome; light from the side like a window.
recipe.why: Food is still — spend shutter, not ISO, and keep ISO at base for clean tones. f/4 gives selective focus on the hero bite; stop toward f/8 when the whole plate must read. Side light mimics window light and builds the shadows that give dishes shape.

watch_fors: Orange tungsten or green fluorescent cast — restaurants are mixed-light traps; fix WB before styling.
Glossy sauces and plates clipping to white — speculars blow before the food looks bright.
Everything sharp including the props — shallow depth is what separates food photos from snapshots.

exercises.title: Hero bite
exercises.goal: Choose what stays sharp on the plate.
exercises.how: At f/4 pick one region — the garnish, the cut interior, the drip — and focus there. Walk to f/8 and compare which version makes you hungry.

exercises.title: Window side-light
exercises.goal: Build shape with one soft directional source.
exercises.how: Rotate the plate (or the simulated light) from front-lit to side-lit to back-lit; watch texture appear in the shadows. Side light sells texture; front light sells flatness.

styles.label: Concert
styles.description: Live music in dark venues with strobing, saturated stage light. The camera fights for every stop: fast glass, high ISO tolerance, and shutter control between freeze and motion energy.

recipe.summary: Widest glass, 1/250 for the performer, ISO ride the lighting desk's mood swings.
recipe.why: Stage light is theatrical: one song spans spotlight and blackout. Wide aperture grabs the stops the venue won't give, 1/250 holds a singing performer while hinting at motion in the hands, and ISO 3200+ is simply the cost of admission — grain beats missing the moment.

watch_fors: Red and blue gels crushing skin tones — expose for the face and let the stage go graphic.
Beams and haze fooling the meter — spot meter the performer, not the light show.
Frozen-but-ghosted faces from slow shutter — 1/250 minimum for the lead, blur is for the drum kit.

exercises.title: One song, three looks
exercises.goal: Ride the light instead of fighting it.
exercises.how: Shoot the same performer through a song change: expose the spotlight, then the blackout, and watch how far ISO and shutter travel. Venue lighting is a moving target — plan for swings, not a setting.

exercises.title: Motion with intent
exercises.goal: Use 1/60 drag for energy where freeze kills the vibe.
exercises.how: Drop to 1/60 and track the guitarist — sharp face, smeared hands. That's the concert look fast shutter can't give you.

styles.label: Real Estate
styles.description: Interiors and exteriors for listings. Straight verticals, window views that hold detail, and honest color — the technical genre where tripods and bracketing beat drama.

recipe.summary: Tripod, base ISO, f/8, slow shutter; expose for the windows and lift the room.
recipe.why: Rooms are still and must be corner-to-corner sharp: f/8 and base ISO on a tripod. The dynamic-range problem — bright windows vs dim interior — is solved with slow shutter plus highlight protection, or bracketing when even that fails.

watch_fors: Windows blown to pure white — they read as 'no view'; protect them and lift the interior instead.
Converging walls and tilted verticals — keep the camera level; fix perspective in framing, not rescue.
Mixed lamp + daylight color — pick one temperature or light the room to match the windows.

exercises.title: Window rescue
exercises.goal: Hold the view while keeping the room readable.
exercises.how: Use exposure comp −1 EV until the histogram's right edge unhooks, then note how the room darkens — that gap is what HDR bracketing exists to fill.

exercises.title: Corner discipline
exercises.goal: Shoot a room so walls stay vertical.
exercises.how: Frame from chest height, camera level, one wall parallel to the frame. Compare with a hand-held tilt — the slant is subtle on the LCD and glaring on a listing.

styles.label: Pets
styles.description: Dogs, cats and every unpredictable companion. Wildlife rules at living-room distances: fast shutter for sudden movement, wide aperture, and focus locked on the eyes.

recipe.summary: Shutter first like sports — 1/500+, wide aperture, ISO whatever it takes.
recipe.why: Pets invent motion: a nap becomes a sprint in half a second. Choose shutter before anything else, open the aperture to lift the pet off a busy floor, and spend ISO freely — noise cleans up in post; a missed expression is gone for good.

watch_fors: Sharp nose, soft eyes — focus discipline: the eyes carry the whole photo.
Shutter crept below 1/250 during play — freeze fails exactly when the pose peaks.
Busy household background — drop the aperture wider or change your angle to a plain wall.

exercises.title: Eye rule
exercises.goal: Prove the eyes carry pet portraits.
exercises.how: Simulate focus on the nose, then the eyes. The f/2.8 falloff makes the difference brutal — build the reflex to check eyes before pressing.

exercises.title: Sprint budget
exercises.goal: Price a freeze in ISO.
exercises.how: Set 1/1000 for the zoomies and watch what ISO it costs indoors. Decide your ceiling before the pet decides your shutter.

styles.label: Family & Kids
styles.description: Children, babies and family groups — portraits with a moving target. Fast shutter for unpredictability, gentle depth, and patience doing the work exposure can't.

recipe.summary: 1/250 floor for toddlers, f/2.8 for gentle separation, ISO rides the room.
recipe.why: Kids move in bursts and blink at the wrong moment: a 1/250 floor catches the peek-a-boo peak. f/2.8 separates faces from birthday-party chaos while keeping both eyes of the group in focus, and ISO 400–1600 is a fair trade for a real expression.

watch_fors: Shutter dropped to 1/60 indoors — toddler speed makes that a motion-blur lottery.
Faces in open shade while the yard glows — expose the faces, let the background do what it wants.
Group depth too thin at f/1.8 — two rows of people need f/2.8–f/4 or the back row softens.

exercises.title: Burst anticipation
exercises.goal: Catch the expression peak, not the aftermath.
exercises.how: Pick 1/500 and simulate a giggle fit; the teaching point is rhythm — kids cycle still-burst-still, and the burst is where the keeper lives.

exercises.title: Party background triage
exercises.goal: Tame chaos with aperture and angle.
exercises.how: At f/2.8 note the melt; step to f/5.6 and watch the clutter return. Depth of field is your cleanup crew when the room won't cooperate.

styles.label: Wedding
styles.description: One-shot documentary work across church dark, dance-floor chaos and outdoor light — often within the same hour. Event skills at their most unforgiving: no retries on the moments that matter.

recipe.summary: f/2.8 safety, 1/160 floor, ISO climbs to 6400 without apology.
recipe.why: Aisle light, reception tungsten and midday sun all arrive uninvited. f/2.8 keeps faces lifted from dim venues, 1/160 protects the first kiss from handheld drift, and ISO 6400 is cheaper than a moment that never happened.

watch_fors: White dress clipping in sunlight — it's the largest bright surface in the frame; protect its texture.
Tungsten reception turning everything amber — the cast lands on skin, where nobody forgives it.
Dark venue + slow shutter — 1/160 floor; motion blur on the kiss is forever.

exercises.title: Dress first
exercises.goal: Protect the one white surface that must survive.
exercises.how: Drop exposure comp until the dress histogram edge unhooks; watch the suit and venue follow. Weddings are highlight management with people attached.

exercises.title: Venue crossover
exercises.goal: Move from church dark to outdoor sun without a casualty.
exercises.how: Simulate stepping outside: ISO 1600 → 100, shutter up, aperture held. The triangle changes three dials in four seconds — rehearse the order.

styles.label: Automotive
styles.description: Cars as sculpture: controlled reflections, rolling or parked. Highlights and color are the whole game — paint lives or dies on what the body reflects.

recipe.summary: Polarizer mindset, f/5.6, 1/500 rolling or tripod stills at base ISO.
recipe.why: Paint is a mirror — every panel reflects the world you point it at. f/5.6 holds the whole car, 1/500 freezes a rolling shot crisply, and base ISO keeps body-color gradations free of noise banding.

watch_fors: You, the horizon and the grid reflected down the door — walk the angles before touching settings.
Hot speculars on chrome blowing to white — they're small but they read as damage.
Panning shots frozen wheels — rolling shots want 1/60–1/125 with the car tracked, wheels blurring.

exercises.title: Reflection walk
exercises.goal: See what the car sees.
exercises.how: Simulate a glossy body and move the light angle; watch highlights slide across panels. The best car photos are made walking the car, then choosing settings.

exercises.title: Rolling at 1/80
exercises.goal: Pan so the car is sharp and the world streaks.
exercises.how: Drop the shutter to 1/80 and track the body; motion in the background sells speed that 1/1000 erases.

styles.label: Aerial & Drone
styles.description: Photography from drones, planes and helicopters. High platform, high vibration, huge vistas: fast shutter to defeat aircraft shake, base ISO for clean skies, and geometry as the subject.

recipe.summary: 1/500 against vibration, f/4–f/5.6, base ISO; treat the horizon as a spirit level.
recipe.why: The aircraft vibrates even when your hands are steady: 1/500 stays ahead of prop and rotor shake. f/4 on a tiny sensor is already deep focus, base ISO keeps big skies gradation-clean, and sunlight from above is bright — spend shutter, not ISO.

watch_fors: Fine texture smeared by vibration — the Nd-filter/slow-shutter combo needs a very steady platform.
Horizon tilted a degree — invisible on the small screen, permanent in the print.
Sky-to-land brightness gap — expose the land, watch the sky edge, consider a gradient in post.

exercises.title: Vibration floor
exercises.goal: Find the shutter where platform shake stops mattering.
exercises.how: Step shutter from 1/125 to 1/1000 and watch fine detail — field texture, roof lines. The stop where crispness locks in is your minimum airborne.

exercises.title: Geometry first
exercises.goal: Compose with lines only a map sees.
exercises.how: Note how roads, shorelines and field edges become the subject from above; depth of field stops mattering when everything is far away.

styles.label: Black & White
styles.description: Mono as a discipline, not a filter. With color gone, exposure becomes tonal placement — light, shape and texture carry everything the palette used to.

recipe.summary: Expose for the tones you want, not the colors you see; ISO 100–400 for clean grays.
recipe.why: In mono, luminance is the only story: place shadows where they give shape, protect the whites that carve form. f/5.6 keeps texture honest, and clean low-ISO grays matter because noise reads as grit in tonal transitions.

watch_fors: Two different colors landing as one gray — separation must come from light, not hue.
Flat mid-gray everything — no true black or clean white means no tonal spine.
Color cast in the capture distorting channel mix — WB accuracy still matters before conversion.

exercises.title: Tonal spine
exercises.goal: Put a true black and a clean white in every frame.
exercises.how: Watch the histogram for both walls being approached without touching them — that spread is what makes mono pop.

exercises.title: Light over color
exercises.goal: Choose scenes by contrast, not by color appeal.
exercises.how: Simulate a colorful sunset scene in mono and watch what survives — the lesson is to hunt light geometry (raking light, hard shadows) instead of palettes.

styles.label: Travel
styles.description: Places, people and light on the move — one bag, no reshoots. The genre is adaptability: scene changes every ten minutes, so settings must follow subject, not habit.

recipe.summary: f/5.6 all-rounder, 1/125 floor for handheld walking, ISO flexible to 1600.
recipe.why: Travel means midday plazas, dim temples and dusk markets in one afternoon. f/5.6 keeps scenes readable, 1/125 stays ahead of walking-pace handheld shake, and ISO 400–1600 is the flexibility budget that keeps you from carrying a tripod.

watch_fors: Harsh noon sun flattening faces — move subjects into shade; the landmark can keep the sun.
Souvenir-shop clutter crowding the landmark — step sideways, drop aperture, or get closer.
Camera shaking at 1/30 after a long day — the floor is 1/125 handheld; rest or brace.

exercises.title: Three scenes, one walk
exercises.goal: Re-derive settings from the subject every ten minutes.
exercises.how: Cycle street → landmark → interior presets and narrate which dial leads each time: shutter for the market, aperture for the monument, ISO for the temple. Travel skill is switching, not perfecting.

exercises.title: Shade relocate
exercises.goal: Fix people with placement before settings.
exercises.how: Simulate harsh sun on a portrait, then move the subject to building shade — exposure evens out for free. Position is the first dial.

styles.label: Product
styles.description: Commercial shots of objects for catalogs and stores. Tripod, controlled light, honest color and edge-to-edge sharpness — precision work where consistency is the deliverable.

recipe.summary: Tripod base ISO, f/8 for full-object sharpness, slow shutter fine; light the set, not the camera.
recipe.why: Product buyers judge texture, edges and true color: f/8 holds the whole object past its focal plane, base ISO keeps gradients spotless, and since nothing moves the shutter can be whatever the lights need. Accuracy beats drama — this genre's drama IS accuracy.

watch_fors: Mixed color temperatures lying about the product color — clients return items that look wrong.
Dust and fingerprints screaming at 100% — clean the set before blaming the lens.
Specular hot spots on gloss — diffuse or flag the light; hot spots read as defects.

exercises.title: Color honesty
exercises.goal: Hold true color across a set.
exercises.how: Simulate a WB shift and watch a white label drift cream or blue — product color is a contract, so WB is set, not guessed.

exercises.title: Edge audit
exercises.goal: Prove the whole object is sharp.
exercises.how: At f/2.8 check the far edge, then step to f/8 and re-check — catalog work has no focal-plane excuses.
